STL Import 1 —
Repairing and Combining STL Files 1
1. The STL geometry is provided courtesy of Mark Yeoman, Continuum Blue, UK.
2 | STL IMPORT 1 —  REPAIRING AND COMBINING STL FILES
Introduction
When working with imported STL meshes, there is often a need to repair and edit the 
mesh, form different computational domains, remesh the faces to improve the element 
quality, and to fill the domains with a volumetric mesh. In case you have several STL files, 
you may also need to modify the position of some of the meshes to remove gaps and 
intersections before combining the meshes.
This tutorial series consists of two parts, where this first part focuses on using available 
tools to edit imported STL meshes: the different operations for repairing the meshes, 
combining imported meshes with each other, and generating a volume mesh from the 
imported surface mesh. The second part of the series, STL Import 2 —  Combining 
Geometry with an Imported Mesh , describes a workflow for combining the mesh obtained 
in the first part with a parameterized geometry.
Figure 1: Left: Tetrahedral mesh after repairing, combining and partitioning imported 
surface meshes in the first part of the tutorial series. Right: Tetrahedral mesh after combining 
the mesh from the first part with parameterized geometry created in the second part of the 
tutorial series.
The STL file format is one of the standard file formats for 3D printing, and it is also often 
used as a format for exchanging 3D scan data. STL files contain only the triangulated 
surface, which can also be called a surface mesh, of a 3D object. The triangles in the file 
are identified by their normals and vertex coordinates and are stitched together using a 
tolerance to form a faceted representation of the object.
COMSOL Multiphysics supports a variety of operations, for example, moving, scaling and 
rotating an imported mesh, combining the imported mesh with parameterized geometry 
to run parametric sweeps, and generating unstructured, structured, and boundary layer 
mesh in the domains. When creating geometry or importing CAD files for combining with 
an imported mesh, you can view the imported mesh with the geometry to help with 

3 | STL IMPORT 1 —  REPAIRING AND COMBINING STL FILES
positioning the design. This procedure is shown in the second part of this tutorial series, 
STL Import 2 —  Combining Geometry with an Imported Mesh .
Lastly, it is important to mention that the workflows presented in this tutorial series apply 
to any type of imported surface meshes, such as the formats PLY and 3MF. They also apply 
when creating a mesh from a Filter or Partition dataset, which you would do when using 
the results of a simulation as the mesh for a new simulation, for example during a topology 
optimization study.
Model Definition
In this tutorial, you will import STL files with surface meshes of the C3,C4 and C5 
vertebrae, as well as the C3-C4 and C4-C5 intervertebral discs.
Figure 2: Imported STL meshes of three vertebrae and intervertebral discs that are used as a 
starting point for this tutorial.
The goal of this tutorial is to demonstrate a workflow for repairing and combining the 
imported surface meshes such that you can create five connected domains that can be filled 
with a tetrahedral mesh. The instructions also detail how to further simplify the imported 

4 | STL IMPORT 1 —  REPAIRING AND COMBINING STL FILES
meshes when you can assume that the problem is symmetric, and how to build a physics-
controlled mesh.
To achieve this, the tutorial includes the following steps:
• Importing the STL files
 Identifying and repairing small defects such as gaps and intersecting elements to obtain 
watertight meshes for creating computational domains
 Moving the meshes into position before combining them
 Uniting the meshes
 Resolving intersections and gaps after the union
 Partitioning the domains with a plane and deleting domains you do not need
 Building a physics-controlled mesh

2 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
Introduction
When working with imported STL meshes, you may run into applications where you want 
to combine your imported mesh with an imported CAD part, CAD assembly, or with 
geometry created in COMSOL Multiphysics.
This tutorial series consists of two parts, where the first part, STL Import 1 —  Repairing 
and Combining STL Files , focuses on using available tools to edit imported STL meshes: 
the different operations for repairing the meshes, combining imported meshes with each 
other, and generating a volume mesh from the imported surface mesh. This second part 
of the series describes a workflow for combining the mesh obtained in the first part with a 
parameterized geometry.
Figure 1: Left: Tetrahedral mesh after repairing, combining, and partitioning imported 
surface meshes in the first part of the tutorial series. Right: Tetrahedral mesh after combining 
the mesh from the first part with parameterized geometry created in the second part of the 
tutorial series.
The STL file format is one of the standard file formats for 3D printing, and it is also often 
used as a format for exchanging 3D scan data. STL files contain only the triangulated 
surface, which can also be called a surface mesh, of a 3D object. The triangles in the file 
are identified by their normals and vertex coordinates and are stitched together using a 
tolerance to form a faceted representation of the object.
COMSOL Multiphysics supports a variety of operations, for example, moving, scaling and 
rotating an imported mesh, combining the imported mesh with parameterized geometry 
to run parametric sweeps, and generating unstructured, structured, and boundary layer 
mesh in the domains. When creating geometry or importing CAD files for combining with 
an imported mesh, you can view the imported mesh with the geometry to help with 
positioning the design. This procedure is shown in the instructions of this tutorial.

3 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
Lastly, it is important to mention that the workflows presented in this tutorial series apply 
to any type of imported surface meshes, such as the formats PLY and 3MF. They also apply 
when creating a mesh from a Filter or Partition dataset, which you would do when using 
the results of a simulation as the mesh for a new simulation, for example during a topology 
optimization study.

first part of this tutorial series, with the geometry of the three pedicle screws and a rod. 
The screws are created as parameterized geometry parts with the possibility of varying the

fill in the table.
5 Locate the Selections of Resulting Entities section. Select the Resulting objects selection 
checkbox.
6 Locate the Assigned Attributes section. Select the Construction geometry checkbox.
7 Click Build Selected.
Rod domain
1 In the Geometry toolbar, click Sweep.
2 In the Settings window for Sweep, type Rod domain in the Label text field.
3 Locate the Cross Section section. From the Entities to sweep list, choose 
Rod cross section.

14 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
4 Clear the Create cross-sectional faces checkbox.
5 Locate the Spine Curve section. From the Edges to follow list, choose Polygon 1.
6 Locate the Selections of Resulting Entities section. Select the Resulting objects selection 
checkbox.
7 Locate the Assigned Attributes section. From the Construction geometry list, choose Off.
8 Click Build Selected.
Delete Entities 1 (del1)
The geometry is almost finished, just some cleanup left to do. First, delete the help points 
as they are no longer needed.
1 In the Model Builder window, right-click Geometry 1 and choose Delete Entities.
2 In the Settings window for Delete Entities, locate the Entities or Objects to Delete 
section.
3 From the Geometric entity level list, choose Object.
4 From the Selection list, choose Help Points.
5 Click Build Selected.
Form Union (fin)
1 In the Model Builder window, click Form Union (fin).

15 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
2 In the Settings window for Form Union/Assembly, click Build Selected.
This removes all construction geometry and you are left with the screws and rod. Check 
the Selection List that there are now four domains, one for each screw and one for the 
rod.
Simplify the boundaries of the screw threads to one single boundary using virtual 
operations.
Form Composite Faces 1 (cmf1)
1 In the Geometry toolbar, click Virtual Operations and choose Form Composite Faces.
2 In the Settings window for Form Composite Faces, locate the Input section.
3 From the Faces to composite list, choose Simplify threads.
4 Click Build Selected.
COMBINED VERTEBRAE AND SCREWS
The geometry is now completed. Next, import it into the meshing sequence and combine 
it with the mesh of the vertebrae and disc.
Import - Geometry
1 In the Model Builder window, under Component 1 (comp1) > Meshes > 
Combined Vertebrae and Screws click Import - Geometry.
2 In the Settings window for Import, locate the Import section.
3 From the Size list, choose Finer.
4 Select the Resolve geometric details checkbox to use a finer element size to represent the 
screws and rod.
This step is done to ensure that the intersecting mesh surfaces of the pedicle screws and 
the vertebrae have a similar element size. This will help with forming the union of the 
meshes further ahead.

16 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
5 Click Import.
This imports the geometry of the screws and rod. Make sure that the screws are indeed 
fully inside the vertebrae by examining the mesh in the Graphics window. If not, go back 
and check that the geometry is set up correctly.
Information
A subnode to the Import - Pedicle screws and rod node informs that the meshes are 
intersecting.
1 In the Model Builder window, click Information.
2 In the Settings window for Information, locate the Information section.
3 From the Select location list, choose Location 5 (0.4007, 20.37, -55.37).
4 Click Center at Coordinates to zoom in on a reported problem coordinate to inspect the 
intersection more closely. If the mesh is more complex, it can help to also clip around 
the coordinates to remove everything except the mesh closest to the coordinates from 
the view and you can also rotate the mesh such that you see at least some of the reported 

17 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
points more clearly. Note that the list of reported points is filtered so that only a smaller 
number of intersecting elements are listed.
Union 1
As suggested in the Information node, use a mesh Union operation to compute the 
intersections.
1 In the Mesh toolbar, click Booleans and Partitions and choose Union.
2 In the Settings window for Union, locate the Cleanup section.
3 From the Placement of mesh vertices list, choose Linear.

18 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
4 Click Build Selected to unite the entire mesh using the default tolerance.
The union has partitioned the faces and the domains at the intersections. Along the new 
edges, some sliver triangles have been created. When building the physics-controlled 
mesh, the quality of the boundary mesh will be improved.
Next, build the physics-controlled mesh.
PHYSICS-CONTROLLED MESH
1 In the Model Builder window, expand the Component 1 (comp1) > Meshes > Physics-
Controlled Mesh node.
2 Right-click Physics-Controlled Mesh and choose Build All.
3 Click the Transparency button in the Graphics toolbar.

19 | STL IMPORT 2 —  COMBINING GEOMETRY WITH AN IMPORTED MESH
4 In the Model Builder window, click Physics-Controlled Mesh.
You have now obtained a volume mesh for the combined vertebrae, discs, and pedicle 
screws.

安装验证
applications.installation verification
This Application is licensed under the COMSOL Application License 6.4.
All trademarks are the property of their respective owners. See www.comsol.com/trademarks.
Application created in COMSOL Multiphysics 6.4
Installation Verification
2 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
About the Installation Ve rification Application
The Installation Verification application can be used to help verify that your COMSOL 
Multiphysics® or COMSOL Server™ installation works as expected on your hardware 
platforms and operating systems. The app automatically loads and runs a suite of test 
models and compares the results with stored expected values. One set of tests compares 
the currently computed results with published results obtained from either experiments or 
other types of computations or analytical results. Another set of tests compares the 
computed results with previously computed stored results, usually with a refined mesh. 
The most computationally demanding test models may require up to 32 GB of RAM.
There are a number of reasons why you may want to run the Installation Verification app 
test suite. For instance, it may help with detecting hardware issues, such as malfunctioning 
memory units, or determine if the system you are running on has been corrupted by a 
malfunctioning software update. Moreover, it will indicate whether the software will run 
or not if you intend to use a platform configuration that is not officially supported.
RUNNING THE APPLICATION
To run the Installation Verification application, first start COMSOL Multiphysics. Then, 
select the 
Run Application option from the File menu, as shown in the figure below. Next, 
browse to the location of the MPH-file installation_verification.mph and open the 
file.

3 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
This opens the application user interface as shown in the figure below.
To run the application, click either of the buttons Quick Run, Run Selected, or Run All.
The Quick Run option runs only models that each take at most 25 s on the reference 
computer. This 25 s default maximum Quick run threshold can be lowered by the user. Run 
Selected runs only the models that have been selected in the Test Suite Models table. Run All 
runs all models. You can see the estimated total time to run the test suite at the top of the 
Test Suite Models table.

4 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
When the test suite starts, you will see a progress bar and the Test Results Table being 
updated with the result of each test, as shown in the figure below.
You can also run the app from the command line with a limited set of options. For more 
information see, Running From the Command Line.
PRODUCTS
When the app first starts, you will see a table of test models. The number of available test 
models depends on the number of products that you have installed. Not all products have 
test models associated with them. The current version of the application includes test 
models for the following products:
CATEGORY PRODUCT
Platform Product COMSOL Multiphysics
Electromagnetics AC/DC Module
Electromagnetics RF Module
Electromagnetics Wave Optics Module
Structural & Acoustics Structural Mechanics Module
Structural & Acoustics Nonlinear Structural Mechanics Module
Structural & Acoustics Multibody Dynamics Module
Structural & Acoustics MEMS Module
Structural & Acoustics Acoustics Module

5 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
Note that due to the way that COMSOL Multiphysics and its add-on products are 
structured, some of the tests are simultaneously applicable to several products.
Fluid & Heat CFD Module
Fluid & Heat Polymer Flow Module
Fluid & Heat Heat Transfer Module
Chemical Chemical Reaction Engineering Module
Chemical Battery Design Module
Multipurpose Optimization Module
Interfacing CAD Import Module
Interfacing Design Module
Interfacing LiveLink™ for SOLIDWORKS®, LiveLink™ for 
Inventor®, LiveLink for AutoCAD®, LiveLink™ for 
Revit®, Livelink™ for PTC® Creo® Parametric™, 
LiveLink™ for PTC® Pro/ENGINEER®, or LiveLink™ 
for Solid Edge®
CATEGORY PRODUCT
6 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
THE TEST SUITE MODELS TABLE
The figure below shows the user interface and how it appears for a case where many of the 
tested products are available.
The Test Suite Models table has the following columns:
• Enabled: This is whether or not the model will be included in a test suite run
 Model Name: This is typically the same name as the corresponding model in the 
Application Libraries
 Required Products: These are the products required to run the model
 Model Description: This is a short description of the model with a reference to the full 
documentation of the model in the Application Libraries
 Computation Time (s), Reference: This is the expected computation time on the reference 
computer

7 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
Above the Test Suite Model table, the Estimated runtime on reference computer value is 
displayed. This number is updated depending on which models are selected.
The test suite models have corresponding fully documented models in the Application 
Libraries. In some cases, the test models have a reduced number of study types compared 
to the corresponding model in the Application Libraries. This is to keep the computation 
times manageable.
THE RIBBON BUTTONS
The ribbon buttons at the top of the user interface are divided into five groups depending 
on their function:

Run Test Suite
- Quick Run: Run only models that each take at most 25 s on the reference computer
- Run Selected: Run only the models that have been selected
- Run All: Run all models.
 Select Models
- Select All: Select all models.
- Select Quick Run: Select only models below the Quick run threshold input field.
- Deselect All: Deselect all models.
 Test Results Table
- Export Test Results: Export the test results to CSV or Microsoft Excel format. Note 
that the Excel format is only available if you have a license for LiveLink™ for Excel.
- Clear Table: Clear the Test Results Table.
 Help
- Reference Computer: Display information about the reference computer 
specifications.
- Help: Open the Installation Verification app documentation.
 Defaults
- Reset: Reset all user-defined settings to their default values.
8 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
THE TEST RESULTS TABLE
After a test is run, the Test Results Table displays a numbered list of tested quantities as well 
as the number of degrees of freedom and computation time.
The Test Results Table has the following columns:
 Test: This is the consecutive number of a test in the current test suite.
 Status: This is whether the test Passed or Failed. The Status is N/A for rows that do not 
correspond to a test; these rows correspond to Number of degrees of freedom and 
Computation time. A test will pass if the Difference is lower than the Tolerance value, see 
below.
 Model Name: This is the same name as in the Test Suite Models.
 Quantity Name: This is the variable name of the tested quantity.
 Description: This is a short description of the tested quantity.
 Expected Value: This is the expected value of the tested quantity.
 Computed Value: This is the currently computed value of the tested quantity.

9 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
 Difference: This is the relative difference between the Computed Value and Expected Value. 
For more information on difference computations, see Relative and Absolute 
Difference Computations.
 Tolerance: This is the relative tolerance used to determine if the test Passed or Failed. 
For more information about the details of a model, please see the corresponding Model 
Description in the Test Suite Models table.
THE TEST SUMMARY AND SETTINGS WINDOW
The Test Summary and Settings window includes a Test Results Summary section with 
general information on the currently run test suite (if any) and a Performance section with 
information on the performance compared to the reference computer. In addition, this 
10 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
window contains user-defined Settings and Advanced Settings options, as shown in the 
figure below.

11 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
The Test Results Summary Section
At the top of the Test Results Summary section, there is a pass or fail indicator and an

The Performance Section
The Performance section provides information on the total time for the last test run, the 
total time for the same run on the reference computer, and the relative performance of the 
tested computer versus the reference computer. The relative performance is computed as 
follows:
(Runtime on reference computer)/(Runtime on tested computer).
The result is presented as a percentage value, where a value higher than 100% means the 
test runs faster on your computer than the reference computer. For example, if a test on 
your computer returns a value of 200%, this means your computer is twice as fast as the 
reference computer for this test suite.
The Settings Section
In the Settings section (shown below) you can change the number of digits displayed in 
the Test Results Table and their presentation format.
The Number of digits can be set between 2 and 16. You can change the number of digits 
even after a test has been finalized. To update the display in the Test Results Table, click the 
button to the right of the text field or anywhere outside the Settings window.
You can select or deselect the Use percent for difference and tolerance checkbox to control 
whether the differences and tolerances are displayed as percentages.
You can choose whether to Include computation time and Include number of degrees of 
freedom in the results by using the corresponding checkboxes.
If you select the Append test results to table checkbox, previously obtained test results will 
be kept in the table and the new results will be appended to the end of the table.

C:\Users\<username>\.comsol\v64\applications\files\common.

box, accessible from the File menu.
The Quick run threshold displays the time used as a threshold for including a test model in

below this threshold will be included in a Quick Run.

The Advanced Settings Section
In the Advanced Settings section, shown in the figure below, you can change low-level 
settings that control how the test suite is run.
The Mesh refinement level option enables you to run certain models with a uniform mesh 
refinement level with values from 0 to 3. The default value is 0, which means that no mesh 
refinement is used. In order for this setting to be available for a model, the model’s 
corresponding verification variable settings need to be set to a value higher than 0. The 
Mesh refinement level option can be useful if you are adding your own test models to the 
test suite and want to perform a mesh refinement study. A model's verification variables 
file controls whether or not mesh refinement is enabled for the model. For more 
information, see The Verification Variables File.
The Run mesh refinement study, starting from 0 checkbox will loop over all available mesh 
refinement levels for a model starting at 0 and solve repeatedly for incremental refinement

levels until the maximum number of refinement levels is reached. The maximum number 
of mesh refinements is 3, unless a lower value has been set by the model's verification 
variable settings.
The Perturbation of values setting can be used to force tests to fail. The value entered is 
treated as a relative factor of the computed value, so the computed value will be multiplied 
by this factor. For example, a value of 1.1 means the computed value will be increased by 
10%, and, depending on the tolerance, may trigger a change of a test status from pass to 
fail. This setting can be used as a debugging tool when adding your own models to the

C:\Users\<username>\.comsol\v64\applications\files\common. This is useful

The Mesh Refinement Level Variable
In the heat_convention_2d_verification_variables.txt file, the first line contains 
the variable name maxMeshRefinementLevel:
maxMeshRefinementLevel 1 "Max refinement level"
This value sets the maximum number of mesh refinements that the app will apply to a test 
model if the advanced setting Mesh refinement level has a value greater than 0. If you use 
a too-high value, the computation will run out of memory on most computers. The 
maximum value is 3. Note, however, that three uniform refinements in a 3D model for a 
tetrahedral mesh will generate approximately three orders of magnitude more elements. 
This is rarely practical, and many of the 3D models in the default test suite have a value 
lower than 3.
If no line with 
maxMeshRefinementLevel is found, the number of allowed mesh 
refinements is set to 3.
The Number of Degrees of Freedom Variables
In the heat_convention_2d_verification_variables.txt file, the next three lines 
contain information on the number of degrees of freedom in the model, as shown below:
ndofs numberofdofs "Number of degrees of freedom"
ndofs_nominal 690 "Number of degrees of freedom, nominal"
ndofs_tolerance 1000 "Number of degrees of freedom, relative tolerance (%)"
For the built-in test suite, this is only used for information purposes. 
The first line assigns the built-in variable numberofdofs to the variable ndofs. The second 
line assigns the variable ndofs_nominal to the expected number of degrees of freedom 
for the model. The third line assigns a tolerance to the variable ndofs_tolerance. The 
default tolerance is set to 1000, which, by the app, is interpreted as applying no tolerance 
at all. Any number greater than or equal to 1000 will be interpreted in this way, and such 
a test will always be set to the status 
Passed. However, you can optionally apply a tolerance 
to the number of degrees of freedom. Why is the number of degrees of freedom not fixed 
in advanced? Slight changes in the software between versions may change the mesh 
generation and thus generate a different number of degrees of freedom. Even changes to 
the number of cores or changes to the operating system may generate a slightly different 
number of degrees of freedom. This is due to the nature of the computer’s floating point 
operations, which use a finite number of significant digits.
The Physics-Based Test Variables
In the heat_convention_2d_verification_variables.txt file, the next three lines 
contain the physics-based test variables:
21 | INSTALLATION VERIFICATION
Tp intop1(T)-273.15 "Temperature at point in [degC]"
Tp_nomimal 18.25 "Temperature at point, nominal"
Tp_tolerance 0.1 "Temperature at point, relative tolerance (%)"
The first line assigns the temperature at a point to the variable Tp. The operator intop1() 
is an integration operator that computes the integral at a point, along an edge, on a 
surface, or in a domain. Integration over a point is the same thing as evaluating the value 
at that point.
The second line assigns the expected value of 
18.25 (in degrees Celsius) to the variable 
Tp_nominal.
The third line assigns the tolerance 0.1% to the variable Tp_tolerance. The value given 
here is always in percentage.
To add more test quantities you can add additional groups of three lines following the 
same pattern. The first line in such a group always assigns the computed quantity to a 
variable. The second line always contains the expected value, and the third line contains 
the tolerance as a percentage.

In the heat_convention_2d_verification_variables.txt file, the next line contains

computationTime 1.3 "Computation time in [s]"
If you are adding your own models, this number will of course need to be for a reference

The Study Number Variable
The optional studyNumber variable is used for test models with more than one study. The 
test suite will run all of the model's studies in sequence, starting from Study 1, up to 
Study N, where N is the value assigned to the variable 
studyNumber.
If no line with studyNumber is found, a default value of 1 is used.
The Mesh Component Variable
The optional meshComponent variable is used for test models with more than one model 
Component. The value of the meshComponent variable denotes which Component that 
should be used for the (optional) mesh refinement.
If no line with meshComponent is found, a default value of 1 is used.
Optional vs. Required Lines in a Verification Variables File
The following lines are optional in a verification variables file and may occur in any order:
maxMeshRefinementLevel 1 "Max mesh refinement level"
studyNumber 2 "Study number"
studyType 3 "Study type"
meshComponent 2 "Mesh component"
The values shown here are just examples.
The only required lines in a verification variables file are those for the number of degrees 
of freedom and computation time. For example, this is a valid verification variables file:
ndofs numberofdofs "Number of degrees of freedom"
ndofs_nominal 690 "Number of degrees of freedom, nominal"
ndofs_tolerance 1000 "Number of degrees of freedom, relative tolerance (%)"
computationTime 1.3 "Computation time in [s]"

关于 “安装验证” App
“安装验证”App 可用于帮助验证您的 COMSOL Multiphysics® 或 COMSOL Server™ 安
装是否能在硬件平台和操作系统上正常运行。本 App 会自动加载并运行一套测试模

的存储结果 （通常采用细化网格）进行比较。计算要求最高的测试模型可能需要高达 
32 GB 的内存。
运行 “安装验证”App 测试套件有很多好处。例如，它可以帮助检测硬件问题，如内

在 heat_convention_2d_verification_variables.txt 文件中，接下来的三行包含

会改变网格生成情况，从而产生不同的自由度数。即使是内核数变化或操作系统变化
也可能会产生略微不同的自由度数，这是由计算机浮点运算的性质决定的，它使用有

第一行将某个点的温度指派给变量 Tp。运算符 intop1() 是一个积分运算符，用于计

第三行将容差 0.1% 指派给变量 Tp_tolerance。这里给出的值总是以百分比形式表
示。
若要添加更多的测试物理量，您可以按照相同的模式再添加三行组成的组。此类组中
的第一行总是将计算的物理量指派给变量，第二行总是包含期望值，第三行包含百分
比形式的容差。

quickrun 选项运行的测试套件仅包含预计运行时间低于快速运行阈值的模型。快速运
行阈值默认为 25s，您可以使用第二个输入变元 runtime 来更改该值。例如，
命
令：
comsol -run installation_verification.mph -appargnames runmode,runtime 
-appargvalues quickrun,10.0
将运行一个包含所有模型的测试套件，预计运行时间为 10.0s。
有关从命令行运行 App 的一般信息，请参阅 Application Builder Reference Manual 。

2 | THIN-FILM RESISTANCE
Introduction
When modeling transport by diffusion or conduction in thin layers, large differences in 
dimensions of the different domains are common. If the model has a sandwich structure, 
you can replace the thinnest layers with a thin-layer approximation, provided that the 
difference in thickness is large.
Model Definition
This study explains the principle of the thin-layer approximation in direct current 
conduction problems. A comparison of a structure with three domains to a simplified 
model that replaces the domain in the middle with a thin-layer approximation shows the 
benefit of this approach (see Figure 1).
Figure 1: Exact domain description (left) and approximation (right). The current flows from 
the base plate to the circular plate on the upper surface of the device.

structure:

there is a substantial difference in conductivity between the thin and thicker layers of the

boundaries are insulated.

In the thin-film approximation the potential is discontinuous at the film boundary. Use 
the Contact Impedance node on interior boundaries to model a thin layer of resistive 
material.
It is also possible to derive the expression for the current density in Equation 7 by 
approximating the gradient using the potential difference over the thin layer. This example 
includes the previous tedious derivation to show that this is exactly what you obtain from 
the solution of Equation 2.
The approximation presented in this example is not limited to direct current problems. 
You can also use it for modeling of diffusion, heat conduction, flow through porous media 
using Darcy’s law, and other types of physics that the divergence of a gradient flux 
describes.
In general, the application of this simplification is appropriate in cases where the 
differences in thickness are so large that the mesh generator cannot even mesh the domain. 
In some cases, the mesh generator might be able to mesh the domain but then creates a 
very large number of elements.
Results and Discussion
Figure 2 shows a comparison between the exact solution of the problem using three 
conductive layers and the thin-film approximation. The comparison reveals an excellent 
agreement in the potential and current distribution despite that the middle film in this 
study is relatively thick. The approximation becomes even more accurate as the film 
thickness between the upper and lower domain decreases.

Created in COMSOL Multiphysics 6.3
Boundary Layer Meshing —
Exploring the Settings
2 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING —  EXPLORING THE SETTINGS
Introduction
A boundary-layer mesh is a type of structured anisotropic mesh where the mesh elements 
have high aspect ratios. For example, in CFD applications close to no-slip wall boundaries, 
the flow is highly anisotropic, and a much finer mesh is needed to resolve high gradients.
With physics-controlled meshing, a boundary-layer mesh is automatically generated for 
fluid-flow applications, and can easily be generated for other applications. In all cases, the 
boundary-layer mesh is inserted after the interior mesh, which means that the interior 
mesh is deformed to accommodate the boundary-layer mesh. This tutorial series focuses 
on the generation and setup of boundary-layer meshes. Throughout the series, we will also 
explore key aspects of boundary-layer meshes, such as the height of the boundary layers, 
the growth rate of elements from the boundary to the interior, and the various techniques 
for corner handling.
In this tutorial, you will learn how to edit the physics-controlled meshing sequence to 
modify the settings for the boundary-layer mesh generation. You will discover the methods 
for controlling the number and distribution of elements in the boundary-layer mesh, and 
the size of the elements by choosing automatic thickness or by specifying the first layer or 
the total boundary layer thickness. We will also show how to control the increase in layer 
thickness from the boundary toward the interior by entering a stretching factor that 
specifies the increase in thickness between two consecutive boundary layers. The tutorial 
also details how to create boundary-layer meshes with different properties on different 
boundaries, how to control the boundary layer generation in sharp corners, and how to 
visualize the mesh to assess the quality of the elements.
The other tutorial in the series, Boundary Layer Meshing — Adding Boundary Layers to 
an Imported Mesh, focuses on boundary-layer mesh generation for an imported mesh, 
including methods for controlling the deformation of the interior mesh. That tutorial also 
explores how to refine the imported mesh before generating the boundary-layer mesh.
3 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING —  EXPLORING THE SETTINGS
Model Definition
MODEL GEOMETRY
The geometry in Figure 1 represents the 2D cross-section of a partially open ball valve in 
a pipe geometry.
Figure 1: The model geometry of the ball valve with approximate angles for the sharp 
corners and the boundary conditions.
DOMAIN EQUATION AND BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
A Laminar Flow interface is used in this tutorial to enable the generation of a physics-
controlled meshing sequence. Figure 1 shows the specified boundary conditions. An Inlet 
boundary condition with an inflow velocity is applied on the left boundary, while an Outlet 
boundary condition is used on the right boundary. All remaining boundaries are wall 
boundaries. Note that we do not solve for the physics; the physics interface is added only 
to generate a physics-controlled meshing sequence that we can use as the starting point for 
exploring the boundary-layer mesh settings.

Modeling Instructions
From the File menu, choose New.
NEW
In the New window, click Model Wizard.
MODEL WIZARD
1 In the Model Wizard window, click 2D.
2 In the Select Physics tree, select Fluid Flow > Single-Phase Flow > Laminar Flow (spf).
3 Click Add.
4 Click Done.
GEOMETRY 1
1 In the Geometry toolbar, click Insert Sequence and choose Insert Sequence.
2 Browse to the model’s Application Libraries folder and double-click the file 
valve_geom_sequence.mph.
3 In the Geometry toolbar, click Build All.
LAMINAR FLOW (SPF)
We begin by adding the inlet and outlet boundary conditions. The boundary layer mesh 
will not be inserted for these boundaries when the physics-controlled mesh is generated.
Inlet 1
1 In the Physics toolbar, click Boundaries and choose Inlet.
2 Select Boundary 1 only.
3 In the Settings window for Inlet, locate the Velocity section.
4 In the U0 text field, type 0.5[m/s].
Outlet 1
1 In the Physics toolbar, click Boundaries and choose Outlet.
2 Select Boundary 8 only.
MESH 1
First, we will build the physics-controlled mesh, as determined by the laminar flow physics 
interface. Later, we will use this as a starting point for exploring the settings for generating 
the boundary layer mesh.

5 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING —  EXPLORING THE SETTINGS
1 In the Model Builder window, under Component 1 (comp1) click Mesh 1.
2 In the Settings window for Mesh, locate the Physics-Controlled Mesh section.
3 From the Element size list, choose Fine.
4 Click Build All.
Examine the mesh. We can see that the mesh is finer where the boundary layer mesh is 
inserted along the wall boundaries. The two corners B, see Figure 1, are meshed with 
even smaller elements than the other wall boundaries.
Next, we will look into the meshing operations that generated the mesh.
5 In the Model Builder window, right-click Mesh 1 and choose Edit Physics-
Induced Sequence.
6 In the Model Builder window, expand the Boundary Layers 1 node.
Boundary Layer Properties 1
You can now see the automatically generated meshing sequence under the Mesh 1 node. It 
consists of the following operations and attributes:
• Size — a global attribute node that controls the size of the elements in the entire 
sequence. A good practice is to use this node to define the coarsest mesh element size 

6 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING —  EXPLORING THE SETTINGS
you plan to have in the geometry. You can then add downstream Size attribute nodes 
as needed to apply finer mesh element size settings on selected entities.
 Size 1 — attribute node to control the element size on specified boundaries. Here, it 
prescribes a finer mesh element size on the wall boundaries.
 Corner Refinement 1 — attribute node that prescribes a mesh refinement at corners 
where the adjacent edges form an angle greater than a specified value. It is usually 
applied to increase the number of elements around corners where the boundary layer 
mesh is trimmed.

Free Triangular 1 — mesh operation to generate an unstructured triangular mesh in the 
simulation domain.
 Boundary Layers 1 — mesh operation to insert a boundary layer mesh for selected 
domains. Contains settings for boundary layer generation in sharp corners.
 Boundary Layer Properties 1 — local attribute node that contains the selection of 
boundaries where the boundary layer mesh should be inserted. It also includes settings 
for layer height and number of layers. Several nodes can be added to specify different 
boundary layer characteristics on different boundaries.
1 In the Model Builder window, under Component 1 (comp1) > Mesh 1 > Boundary Layers 1 
click Boundary Layer Properties 1.
7 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING —  EXPLORING THE SETTINGS
2 Zoom in around corner C, see Figure 1, in the top right region of the valve to see the 
inserted boundary layers mesh more clearly.
The boundary layer mesh generated for the laminar flow model consists of two layers of 
quad elements inserted into the triangular mesh that has been deformed to 
accommodate the boundary layers. The quad elements have a large aspect ratio, with 
long element sides several times larger than the short sides. This anisotropy is desired 
for resolving the variable fields close to the boundaries. Much higher aspect ratios, even 
close to 100, can be acceptable for solving the equations. Despite the anisotropy these 
elements have quite good quality since the edges of the quad elements are close to 
perpendicular.
Other important characteristics of boundary layer meshes are the element thickness and 
the growth rate for the thickness from the boundary to the interior. Especially for fluid 
flow applications, the element size should increase as little as possible between layers. In 
the current mesh, the thickness of the first boundary layer is only slightly less than that 
of the second layer. Moreover, the triangular mesh has been deformed so that the first 
layer of triangles is only slightly larger than the neighboring quad layer, and the size of 
the triangular elements is then gradually increased toward the interior.
Where the boundary layer mesh wraps around the corner, the element sides are skewed, 
but the quality of these elements is still very good. This could become an issue if the

2 |  边 界 层 网 格 划 分 -  探 索 设 置
简介
边界层网格是一种结构化的各向异性网格，其中网格单元具有高纵横比。例如，在接
近无滑移壁边界的 CFD 应用中，流动的各向异性非常显著，因此需要更细的网格来解
析高梯度区域。
通过物理场控制的网格划分，可以自动创建用于流体流动应用的边界层网格，也可以
轻松生成用于其他应用的边界层网格。无论哪种应用，边界层网格都是在内部网格生
成之后插入的，这意味着，原有的内部网格需要变形以适应插入的边界层网格。本系
列教程侧重于边界层网格的生成和设置。在整个系列教程中，我们还将探讨边界层网
格的一些关键要素，包括边界层的高度、从边界到内部的单元增长率，以及多种拐角
处理方法。
在本教程中，您将学习如何编辑物理场控制网格划分序列，以修改边界层网格的生成
设置。您将了解到如何控制边界层网格中单元的数量及其分布情况，以及如何通过选
择自动厚度或者指定第一层厚度或边界层总厚度来控制单元大小。此外，教程还将介
绍如何通过输入拉伸因子来控制从边界到内部的层厚度增量，该拉伸因子指定了两个
连续边界层之间厚度的增量。教程还详细说明了如何在不同边界上创建具有不同属性
的边界层网格，如何控制尖角处的边界层生成，以及如何通过网格可视化来评估单元
质量。
本系列的另一个教程边界层网格划分 - 在导入的网格中添加边界层，主要介绍如何为导
入的网格生成边界层网格，包括控制内部网格变形的方法。此外，该教程还探讨了如
何在生成边界层网格之前对导入的网格进行细化处理。

Boundary Layer Meshing — Adding Boundary

2 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING — ADDING BOUNDARY LAYERS TO AN IMPORTED 
Introduction
A boundary layer mesh is a type of structured anisotropic mesh where mesh elements have 
high aspect ratios. For example, in CFD applications close to no-slip wall boundaries, the 
flow is highly anisotropic, and a much finer mesh is needed to resolve high gradients.
With physics-controlled meshing, a boundary-layer mesh is automatically generated for 
fluid flow applications, and can easily be generated for other applications. In all cases, the 
boundary-layer mesh is inserted after the interior mesh, which means the interior mesh is 
deformed to accommodate the boundary-layer mesh. This tutorial series focuses on the 
generation and setup of boundary-layer meshes. Throughout the series, we will also 
explore key aspects of boundary-layer meshes, such as the height of the boundary layers, 
the growth rate of elements from the boundary to the interior, and the various techniques 
for corner handling.
This tutorial focuses on creating a boundary-layer mesh for an imported mesh. We will also 
explore how to apply the Refine operation to increase the number of elements in the 
imported mesh without generating a new mesh. You will learn how to configure the 
number and distribution of elements in the boundary layer and how to control the 
deformation of the interior mesh.
The other tutorial in the series, Boundary Layer Meshing —  Exploring the Settings, 
details how to modify the settings for a boundary-layer mesh generated by a physics-
controlled meshing sequence. You will discover how to control the number of layers, 
define the layer thicknesses, and create a boundary-layer mesh with different properties for 
different boundaries. The tutorial also demonstrates the available methods for adding 
boundary layers around corners and the setup of mesh plots for assessing the element 
quality.

We have imported a structured mesh consisting of quad elements. It was built in such

Assume that we would like to increase the number of elements in the imported mesh 
without generating a new mesh. We can easily do this using the Refine operation.
Refine 1
The refine operation splits elements a specified number of times by inserting new mesh 
vertices and edges in the existing elements. It places new and moved mesh vertices on a 
higher-order representation of the faces and edges, which means that a refined mesh will 
resolve curved boundaries.
1 In the Mesh toolbar, click Modify and choose Refine.
2 In the Settings window for Refine, locate the Refine Options section.
3 From the Refinement method list, choose Split longest side.

7 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING — ADDING BOUNDARY LAYERS TO AN IMPORTED
4 Click Build Selected.
The longest side refinement method bisects the longest edge of each element. For a 
regular quad element, as some elements are in the current mesh, the result is a triangle 
and a somewhat skewed quad element. Thus, this method is generally unsuitable for 
nonsimplex meshes because the refinement destroys the structured nature of such 
meshes.
5 From the Refinement method list, choose Regular refinement.

8 | BOUNDARY LAYER MESHING — ADDING BOUNDARY LAYERS TO AN IMPORTED 
6 Click Build Selected.
The regular refinement method bisects each edge of an element. This results in 2dim 
new elements of the same type, where dim is the element dimension. In this case, each 
two dimensional element is split into 4 elements.
You can also see that the refined mesh preserves the curvature of the boundary.

2 |  边 界 层 网 格 划 分 -  在 导 入 的 网 格 中 添 加 边 界 层
简介
边界层网格是一种结构化的各向异性网格，其中网格单元具有高纵横比。例如，在接
近无滑移壁边界的 CFD 应用中，流动的各向异性非常显著，因此需要更细的网格来解
析高梯度区域。
通过物理场控制的网格划分，可以自动创建用于流体流动应用的边界层网格，也可以
轻松生成用于其他应用的边界层网格。无论哪种应用，边界层网格都是在内部网格生
成之后插入的，这意味着，原有的内部网格需要变形以适应插入的边界层网格。本系
列教程侧重于边界层网格的生成和设置。在整个系列教程中，我们还将探讨边界层网
格的一些关键要素，包括边界层的高度、从边界到内部的单元增长率，以及多种拐角
处理方法。
本教程的重点是为导入的网格创建边界层网格。我们还将探讨如何应用 “细化”操作
在不生成新网格的情况下增加导入网格中的单元数。您将学习如何配置边界层中单元
的数量和分布，以及如何控制内部网格的变形。
本系列的另一个教程边界层网格划分 - 探索设置，详细介绍了如何修改由物理场控制网
格划分序列生成的边界层网格的设置。您将了解到如何控制层数、定义层厚度，以及
为不同边界创建具有不同属性的边界层网格。该教程还演示了在拐角处添加边界层的
不同方法，以及如何设置网格图来评估单元质量。

细化 1
细化操作通过在现有单元中插入新的网格顶点和边，将单元按指定次数拆分。这一过
程会将新的和移动过的网格顶点放置在面和边的高阶表示上，这意味着细化后的网格
可以解析弯曲边界问题。
1 在网格工具栏中单击 修改，然后选择细化。

用于非单纯形网格，因为细化过程会破坏这类网格的结构化特性。
